slides.title: Groups decide who can open. Caps decide what they can do.
slides.text: In the first story, Mia and the plumber got into groups. Being in a group means holding its key: you can read. But reading isn't doing. For doing, there's the {cap}: a permission slip, pinned to a group.

slides.title: A cap is a small piece of JSON.
slides.text: Who gets it, on what, and which {ops}. That's the whole shape. Ops are verbs: read, write, share, and anything finer.

slides.title: Every change says what it does.
slides.text: When Mia ticks “buy milk”, her signer signs a {change}: who, which Doc, which op, where. A change is just an op with a signature on it.

slides.title: Every device checks every change.
slides.text: Your laptop, Mia's phone, the street's server: each one asks the same question before it merges a change. Is there a cap that covers this op, for this signer's identity, on this Doc? No cap, no merge. Nobody has to be asked, nobody can be bribed.

slides.title: The plumber may only tick “done”.
slides.text: “write” is the big verb. Ops can be much smaller: one op, on one {path}. The plumber can read the tap item and set its done flag. Change the title? Dropped by every device.

slides.title: The kids can add, but not delete.
slides.text: They may insert new items into the list, and tick done, but only on items they wrote themselves. A {where} narrows an op to the entries that match it.

slides.title: Sharing hands on a smaller slip.
slides.text: {share} is an op too, and it says what may be passed on. Mia can let Grandma read the list, never write it. A slip you hand on can only be the same or smaller, never bigger.

slides.title: Slips can run out.
slides.text: The plumber needs access this week, not forever. {until} ends the cap by itself. After that, every device drops his changes, and the next key rotation shuts him out of reading too.

slides.title: Queries run where the keys are.
slides.text: “What's still open for me?” is a {query}. Your device answers it from what it can already read. No server sees the question or the answer.

slides.title: A cap can point at a query.
slides.text: You want the plumber to see every open plumbing item, now and later. The cap's “on” is a query. Here's the honest part: you can only hide what has its own key. So the owner's device keeps the matching items in their own group, and the plumber is in that group.

slides.title: The server carries, but never reads.
slides.text: The street's server keeps your Docs and passes changes on. Its cap says {store} and {sync}, never read. It is not in the group, so it never holds the key: it moves sealed boxes.

slides.title: Big ops need more than one yes.
slides.text: Deleting the whole house list is serious. The cap says it {needs} both of you. The delete only counts once both signatures are on it.

slides.title: Caps live in the group's own Doc.
slides.text: A group is a Doc too: its members and its caps are entries. Giving a cap is a change. Taking it away is a change. A change counts if a cap covered it in the history it was written on, so a revoke can't erase what came before it.

slides.title: That's the whole system.
list: A group holds the key: who can read.
A cap lists the ops: who can do what.
Every change is one signed op.
Every device checks every change against the caps.
